Title: Surface Sensitivity in Lean 4 Autoformalization
Text:
Surface Sensitivity in Lean 4 Autoformalization
William Feng * 1 Ethan Lou * 1 Aryan Sharma * 1
Abstract
Natural-language variation poses a key challenge
in Lean autoformalization: semantically equiva-
lent paraphrases of the same theorem statements
can induce divergent formal outputs, yet it re-
mains unclear whether this variation reflects se-
mantic disagreements or shallower failures. We
investigate this question in Lean 4 using 60 de-
terministic paraphrase rules applied to ProofNet#
and miniF2F. Across four GPT-family models and
three open-weight 7B autoformalizers, we find
that the observed paraphrase sensitivity reflects
compilation-boundary failures rather than seman-
tic divergence among successful formalizations.
In particular, when both baseline and perturbed
outputs compile, paired predictions are semanti-
cally equivalent under BEq+ and structurally near-
identical under GTED. By contrast, paraphras-
ing substantially affects whether outputs compile,
with failure modes varying across datasets and
perturbation classes. Our results suggest that fu-
ture training-time interventions should target the
compile boundary rather than the semantic layer,
and that benchmarks should separate compile-
conditional equivalence from surface consistency.
1. Introduction
Autoformalization benchmarks (Azerbayev et al., 2023;
Zheng et al., 2022; Poiroux et al., 2025) often evaluate theo-
rems on a single canonical natural language phrasing, even
though model scores can vary substantially across meaning-
preserving paraphrases (Moore & Shah, 2025). This raises
a central question: whether paraphrase-driven variance re-
flects semantic disagreement or failure at a shallower level.
We investigate this question in Lean 4 using a suite of 60
deterministic paraphrase rules applied to ProofNet# and
miniF2F. Each rule is implemented as a regex-based sur-
face trigger and backed by a textbook citation establishing

the intended meaning preservation. These rules edit single,
named linguistic axes (e.g., conditional restructuring, con-
cept renaming), allowing us to attribute paraphrase-driven
variance to specific input features and measure per-category
consistency rates. We coin the term compilation boundary to
refer to the distinction between generated Lean statements
that are accepted by Lean and those rejected because of syn-
tax, elaboration, or identifier errors. This controlled setup
lets us separate semantic disagreement among successful
formalizations from failures at the compilation boundary.
Our main finding is that observed paraphrase sensitivity
in Lean 4 autoformalization reflects compilation-boundary
failures rather than semantic divergence among compiling
outputs. All N=602 paired predictions where both out-
puts compile are BEq+-equivalent across four GPT-family
models and two datasets, and an independent GTED probe
reports median abstract syntax tree (AST) similarity 1.000.
Instead, most inconsistency arises from pairs where at least
one output fails to compile. These compile-boundary fail-
ures are dataset-dependent: unknown identifiers dominate
on ProofNet# whereas syntax and elaboration errors prevail
on miniF2F, and the destabilizing perturbation axis differs
accordingly. This dissociation generalizes beyond the GPT
panel, with three open-weight 7B autoformalizers showing
similar surface inconsistency and compile-boundary fail-
ures.
Together, these results motivate evaluation protocols
that report surface consistency separately from compile-
conditional semantic equivalence, and suggest that future
robustness interventions should address compile-boundary
failures so as to narrow the gap between plausible Lean
generations and compilable Lean formalizations.
2. Related Work
Autoformalization refers to the translation of natural-
language mathematics into a machine-verifiable formal lan-
guage (Wu et al., 2022; de Moura & Ullrich, 2021). Re-
cent work has substantially improved closed- and open-
weight autoformalizers, including those of Lean-oriented
systems (Lu et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b;
Wang et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2025) and retrieval-augmented
approaches for premise selection over Mathlib (Yang et al.,
2023)..

However, these benchmarks evaluate only a single canonical
natural-language phrasing per theorem. This setup makes it
difficult to determine whether inconsistencies across para-
phrases reflect genuine differences in mathematical inter-
pretation or simply failures to produce valid formalizations.
Since generated formalizations can differ syntactically from
benchmark references while expressing the same theorem,
evaluation also requires equivalence metrics such as BEq+
bidirectional proof search, FormalAlign contrastive scor-
ing (Lu et al., 2025), and GTED AST edit distance (Liu
et al., 2025c).
Our work relates to studies of surface robustness under
meaning-preserving input variation in informal mathemat-
ical reasoning (Zhu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Hao
et al., 2025) and NL-to-code translation (Mastropaolo et al.,
2023; Chen et al., 2024). However, autoformalization differs
because correctness is compiler-verified, meaning that in-
consistencies may arise not only from semantic differences
but also from failures to produce syntactically valid code.
Closest to our setting, Moore & Shah (2025) shows that
LLM-generated paraphrases of miniF2F and ProofNet can
change whether outputs compile, and Liu et al. (2025a) doc-
uments identifier hallucination as a major failure mode in
undergraduate-level autoformalization. We build upon this
by using a controlled suite of deterministic paraphrases to
localize failures and show that sensitivity largely stems from
compilation errors rather than differences in mathematical
meaning across seven models.
3. Methods
Perturbations.
We apply 60 named rules to theorem-
statement natural language prose across 11 categories (con-
cept rename, conditional, discourse, quantifier, verbosity,
and others). Math spans ($...$) are masked so LaTeX
formulas and identifiers are never altered. Every rule has
an input pattern, context guards, and a textbook reference
cited for meaning preservation (Appendix B.1). Of these,
14 rules apply on ProofNet# and 37 on miniF2F.1
Datasets.
ProofNet# contributes 185 undergraduate the-
orems that often require nontrivial Mathlib API naviga-
tion to formalize, while miniF2F contributes 244 olympiad
problems paired with standardized Lean formalizations that
closely mirror their natural-language statements.
Models.
We evaluate four GPT-family models (o3, GPT-
5.4, o1, o4-mini) and three open-weight 7B autoformalizers
(Kimina (Wang et al., 2025), Herald (Gao et al., 2025), and
DeepSeek-Prover-V2 (Ren et al., 2025)). Serving details for
the open-weight models are in Appendix B.2.
1All code is available at https://anonymous.4open.
science/r/lean-perturbations-F14C/.
Evaluation metrics.
We use BEq+ (Poiroux et al., 2025)
as the primary equivalence metric because of its published
correlation with human judgment, and GTED (Liu et al.,
2025c) as an independent cross-check on the compile-
both subset.
Non-compiling predictions count as non-
equivalent. We patch BEq+ for preamble-emitting models
(Appendix B.3) and report 95% bootstrap CIs throughout.
Determinism check.
For each GPT model, we issue 50
paired requests with identical inputs and observe byte-
identical outputs in all cases, confirming deterministic be-
havior at the API layer.
4. Results
4.1. Semantic Invariance
Compile-both
outputs
are
BEq+-equivalent.
All
N=602 compile-both paired predictions are BEq+-
equivalent across four models and two datasets, with
no exceptions (Appendix A.1).
The overall surface
consistency is lower, with success rates of 19.1–49.5% on
ProofNet# and 44.5–55.5% on miniF2F across the GPT
panel (Figure 1(a)), well below the 100% byte-identical
agreement we observe on repeated identical inputs (§3).
Compile rates per direction are 11–24%, meaning most
of the inconsistency comes from pairs where at least one
output fails to compile.
GTED cross-check confirms structural near-identity.
We rule out the possibility that BEq+ marks structurally
different outputs as equivalent by using GTED, an AST edit
distance. Surveying o3 on N=43 examples from ProofNet#,
GTED and BEq+ agree on 31/43 pairs (72%). Among the
15 compile-both pairs, the median GTED is 1.000, com-
pared to a mean of 0.532 for the 28 BEq+-non-equivalent
pairs. This shows that compile-both pairs are structurally
near-identical, rather than cases where a permissive scorer
overlooks differences.
Low baseline accuracy does not explain the invariance.
Baseline accuracy against ground truth is low (4.9–11.0%,
N ≈100 each), raising the concern that two mostly-wrong
outputs could agree by coincidence. Two checks rule this
out (Appendix A.3): error rates for ‘baseline-only correct’
and ‘perturbed-only correct’ are within 1% per cell (whereas
coincidence would produce asymmetry), and most “both
wrong” cases are pairs where both outputs fail to compile
rather than wrong-but-compiling outputs that happen to
match. Both checks indicate that the 602/602 equivalence re-
flects true semantic similarity rather than coincident wrong-
ness.

4.2. Compiling Variance
Failures are typed differently by dataset.
On ProofNet#,
34–50% of compile failures are unknown-identifier errors:
for example, the model emits a Mathlib API name that
doesn’t exist in the pinned version, such as SimpleGroup
where the correct identifier is IsSimpleGroup.
On
miniF2F, 22–48% of compile failures are syntax errors and
25–39% are elaboration failures (Appendix A.4): miniF2F
theorems are formalized from scratch, so failures often show
up as broken Lean code rather than wrong library names. In
both cases, perturbations push the model to a made-up iden-
tifier or malformed construction, which Lean then rejects.
The destabilizing axis is dataset-specific.
The destabi-
lizing category differs across datasets (Figure 1(b)). On
ProofNet#, conditional restructuring (“if . . . then” →“when-
ever”) is worst at 25.1%, and discourse, verbosity, and quan-
tifier rephrasing follow at 30–36%. On miniF2F, concept
renaming is the weakest category at 5.0% (N=20, 95% CI
[0.0, 15.0]), an order of magnitude below any ProofNet#
category. Conversely, type/notation rephrasing is the most
stable miniF2F category at 40.2%. The per-category break-
down for miniF2F is in Appendix A.5; the per-rule heatmap
for the GPT panel is in Appendix A.2.
These differences track each dataset’s formalization path-
way. ProofNet# formalizations depend on hypothesis struc-
ture, which requires navigating Mathlib’s typeclass hierar-
chy to select the correct API entry point. As a result, surface
edits that restructure logical form change which API path
the model takes. In contrast, miniF2F formalizations de-
pend on vocabulary, mapping phrases like “sum of the first
n integers” onto specific Lean identifiers. Edits that rename
concepts therefore directly disrupt this lookup.
This dichotomy is consistent with the failure-mode split
documented in Appendix A.4: ProofNet# failures concen-
trate in unknown-identifier errors (34–50% across models),
while miniF2F failures concentrate in syntax and elabora-
tion errors (47–70% combined). The same surface edit can
therefore destabilize different layers of the autoformaliza-
tion pipeline depending on which dataset it targets.
Table 1 shows three concrete failures. In these examples,
the baseline formalization is BEq+-equivalent to the ground-
truth reference, while the perturbed one is not, despite the
underlying mathematical content remaining unchanged.
Open-weight models show the same dissociation.
Three
open-weight 7B autoformalizers scored on the ProofNet#
rules shared with the GPT panel show consistency rates of
19.8–55.6% (Figure 2), within the range spanned by the
GPT panel (19.1–49.5%). This highlights that our compile-
boundary dissociation is not an artifact of GPT-family mod-
els. A 4-gram Jaccard audit against Herald’s released train-
ing corpus shows only 4/185 ProofNet# theorems exceed a
0.5 similarity threshold (mean max-similarity 0.11), indicat-
ing memorization is not the dominant signal; Kimina and
DeepSeek do not publish training data. Per-rule breakdowns
are in Appendix A.6.

5. Discussion
We study paraphrase sensitivity in Lean 4 autoformalization,
and find it to primarily be a compile-boundary phenomenon,
not a semantic one. Specifically, 602/602 pairs where both
outputs compile are semantically equivalent under BEq+
and structurally near-identical under an independent GTED
probe. This dissociation is replicated across three open-
weight 7B autoformalizers, localizing the variance at com-
pilation.
Our findings suggest that compile-conditional equivalence,
i.e., how often outputs agree when both compile, is a distinct
evaluation axis from raw pass rates. Two cleaner reports
follow directly from our setup: (i) how often outputs are
equivalent when both compile, and (ii) how consistent each
model is across paraphrase categories.
5.1. Limitations
Our compile-conditional equivalence claim depends on
BEq+ as the equivalence checker; BEq+ is sound but not
complete, and the o4-mini row of Table 1 shows one case
where bidirectional proof search cannot close a likely-true
equivalence. The 60-rule perturbation suite covers conven-
tional English mathematical paraphrases and underrepre-
sents notational and multilingual edits. Our open-weight
panel is limited to three 7B autoformalizers, and whether
larger or differently-trained models show the same disso-
ciation is open. Finally, we only run GTED cross-check
on N=43 ProofNet# examples from o3; we leave extend-
ing this probe to the other GPT models and open-weight
autoformalizers as future work.
5.2. Future Work
We note that the compile-boundary localization makes spe-
cific training-time interventions feasible, since compile fail-
ures are automatically classifiable signals. The 34–50%
unknown-identifier rate on ProofNet# is directly addressable
by retrieval-augmented identifier resolution or constrained
decoding over Mathlib’s API surface, while the 22–48%
syntax-error rate on miniF2F can be absorbed by fine-tuning
on compiler feedback. We expect interventions narrowly
targeted at the compile boundary to close the gap between
paraphrase-sensitive surface consistency and paraphrase-
invariant semantic capability. We leave this for future work.

A.2. Per-Rule GPT-Panel Heatmap on ProofNet#
Figure 3 gives the per-(rule, model) BEq+ equivalence rates

A.3. Divergence Classification
We classify each paired prediction against the ground-truth
Lean 4 reference into five categories: Both Correct (BC,
both equivalent to the reference), Baseline Only (BL, only
the baseline matches), Perturbed Only (Pert, only the per-
turbed matches), Both Wrong (BW, neither matches), and
Identical (Id, the two predictions are byte-identical). Table 3
gives the full breakdown. BW is the largest category for
every cell (62–83%). BL and Pert are symmetric to within
1pp for every cell: on ProofNet#, BL ranges from 2.0% to
5.6% and Pert from 1.7% to 5.2%.

B. Methodology Details
B.1. Construction-Correctness Spec
Each perturbation rule specifies an input pattern, transforma-
tion, context guards, and a reference establishing meaning
preservation. Rules do not modify content inside math spans
($...$). We mask spans before matching and restore them
after substitution, ensuring LaTeX formulas and variable
names remain unchanged. Rules that fail their guard condi-
tions are skipped. Table 7 shows three representative rules
(conditional, discourse, concept rename).

B.2. Open-Weight Inference Setup
Kimina-Autoformalizer-7B uses the model card chat tem-
plate with system prompt “You are an expert in mathematics
and Lean 4” and a user prompt requesting Lean 4 autofor-
malization with a fixed theorem name. DeepSeek-Prover-V2
uses single-turn completion on the input statement. We set
temperature 0 and max tokens 2048 for both. We extract
only the theorem ...
:= sorry block from each
output.
B.3. BEq+ Wrapper Patch
BEq+ prepends a preamble (import Mathlib plus a
fixed namespace) to each prediction before compilation.
Herald-generated outputs already include their own pream-
ble. When concatenated, duplicate imports cause the Lean
compiler to reject the file. If the wrapper preserves the
prediction preamble, we strip the wrapper preamble before
compilation. Without this step, every Herald pair returns
method=failed due to a wrapper artifact, not model
output.

Abstract: Natural-language variation poses a key challenge in Lean autoformalization: semantically equiva- lent paraphrases of the same theorem statements can induce divergent formal outputs, yet it re- mains unclear whether this variation reflects se- mantic disagreements or shallower failures. We investigate this question in Lean 4 using 60 de- terministic paraphrase rules applied to ProofNet# and miniF2F. Across four GPT-family models and three open-weight 7B autoformalizers, we find that the observed paraphrase sensitivity reflects compilation-boundary failures rather than seman- tic divergence among successful formalizations. In particular, when both baseline and perturbed outputs compile, paired predictions are semanti- cally equivalent under BEq+ and structurally near- identical under GTED. By contrast, paraphras- ing substantially affects whether outputs compile, with failure modes varying across datasets and perturbation classes. Our results suggest that fu- ture training-time interventions should target the compile boundary rather than the semantic layer, and that benchmarks should separate compile- conditional equivalence from surface consistency.
